source: Sabuncu, Boyer, High (2026) BCSER: Capacity Building for Developing a Troubleshooting Learning Environment (ASEE Paper 52353)
finding: Year 1 of an NSF project (grant 2422510) interviewed 18 experienced engineers about how they perceive and manage complexity in troubleshooting. Experts described four complexity categories: system representation, information ambiguity, situational, and stakeholder.
numbers: N=18 engineers, each with over 10 years of experience: 14 industry, 4 academic research. 10 PhD, 2 MS, 6 BS. 17 male, 1 female. Domains: manufacturing, medical devices, robotics, defense, power electronics, software/CAD, academia. Purposive, stratified sample.
limits: Conference paper with preliminary results. No inter-rater figures and no counts per category. Only 1 female participant; authors plan more interviews.
agent_relevance: Complexity is a property of the task and its setting, not only of the fault. Our agent can tag each problem by these four types and pick the matching operator: map the system when representation is the problem, ask for evidence when information is ambiguous.
quote: The experts' reflections revealed four primary categories of complexity

source: Sabuncu, Boyer, High (2026) BCSER: Capacity Building for Developing a Troubleshooting Learning Environment (ASEE Paper 52353)
finding: The authors define complexity as a misalignment between layers (manifolds) of troubleshooting, so that movement toward resolution is blocked or destabilized. Five manifolds: system dynamics, epistemic representation, normative, divergence, situational and stakeholder.
numbers: Worked example: if the divergence and situational manifolds are misaligned and one cannot tell whether the system is faulty at all, that registers as situational complexity. Theory proposal, no tested effect size.
limits: Theoretical framework from preliminary interviews. Not validated, not formalised, no reliability data.
agent_relevance: A useful trigger idea: complexity shows up as a mismatch between layers (what the model says the system does vs what the evidence says vs what the goal requires). A mismatch check in code could fire a state change, in line with G1 (doubt only on a signal).
quote: complexity arises when there is misalignment across layers such that movement toward resolution is blocked or destabilized

source: Sabuncu, Boyer, High (2026) BCSER: Capacity Building for Developing a Troubleshooting Learning Environment (ASEE Paper 52353)
finding: Each manifold has its own governing logic: causal for system dynamics, epistemic for what counts as evidence, evaluative for what counts as resolved, experiential for the point where inadequacy becomes a demand for inquiry, and juridical or organisational for which actions are allowed.
numbers: Definitions given for 5 manifolds. Authors say progress at the system layer is judged by change in behaviour, not by how persuasive an explanation is.
limits: Conceptual. The manifolds are called independent, but no test of that is shown.
agent_relevance: Matches G2 and G3: judge progress by real output, not by how good an explanation sounds. The normative manifold suggests an explicit stop rule (what counts as resolved).
quote: Progress at this layer is assessed through changes in behavior, not through persuasiveness of explanation.

source: Sabuncu, Boyer, High (2026) BCSER: Capacity Building for Developing a Troubleshooting Learning Environment (ASEE Paper 52353)
finding: Think-aloud case: a pneumatic compressor that shuts down intermittently after about 2 minutes. Two participants differed in order of work. JOEY (engineer, 10+ years) sought system understanding first and sketched diagrams. HAZEL (PhD student) sought it only if useful for root-cause analysis and used no visual reasoning.
numbers: 6 participants did think-aloud; 2 reported, both male. Cues were deliberately incomplete. Symptom: shutdown at 20 to 25 psi below the cut-out threshold; motor housing hot; more start-up cycles.
limits: N=2 reported. No outcome scores, so no claim about which order is better. Case intentionally ill-structured.
agent_relevance: Two reasonable orders exist: model first, or cause first. Do not hard-code one. Sketching a block diagram is one operator the senior engineer used.

source: Sabuncu, Boyer, High (2026) BCSER: Capacity Building for Developing a Troubleshooting Learning Environment (ASEE Paper 52353)
finding: Interview coding showed group differences, but the data were too small for statistics. Defense, biomedical and product design engineers reported more situational awareness. Biomedical and product design engineers reported more ambiguity. Engineers with a PhD reported less collaborative problem solving than those with BS or MS.
numbers: Group counts in the paper: defense n=4, biomedical n=8, product design n=13 (groups overlap, since one engineer can carry several industry tags).
limits: Authors say the data are too limited for quantitative analysis. Differences are impressions, not tests.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence that domain shapes which complexity appears. Do not hard-code domain rules from it.

source: Sabuncu, Boyer, High (2026) BCSER: Capacity Building for Developing a Troubleshooting Learning Environment (ASEE Paper 52353)
finding: Troubleshooting is described as non-linear, non-sequential and recursive. Experts orchestrate local tasks (root cause analysis, system modelling) under global manifolds; domain knowledge supplies the syntax. The general frame is divergent exploration of causes then convergent narrowing, with tasks revisited as evidence arrives.
numbers: Rests on 2 temporal codings (Figure 2) plus the interviews. No counts of revisits.
limits: Preliminary.
agent_relevance: Supports a state machine with allowed loops back to earlier states on new evidence, not a one-way pipeline.

source: Sabuncu, Boyer, High (2026) BCSER: Capacity Building for Developing a Troubleshooting Learning Environment (ASEE Paper 52353)
finding: Planned instructional scaffolds are mapped to complexity types: functional block diagrams and flow charts for representation complexity; argument maps and purposeful sampling for information ambiguity.
numbers: Not yet tested. Listed as future work with case studies from real incidents and constructed ones.
limits: No learning outcomes reported yet.
agent_relevance: Candidate operators for our schema: build a functional block diagram; build an argument map over rival causes. Both untested for LLMs.

source: Sabuncu (2026) Developing a Troubleshooting Learning Environment for Complex Engineering Problems (NSF ECR PI meeting poster)
finding: A project poster gives different sample numbers from the paper: semi-structured interviews with 22 experts and think-aloud sessions with 6 expert engineers. Research questions: what constitutes troubleshooting expertise in industry, and how can a learning environment support adaptive skills.
numbers: Interviews n=22 (poster) vs n=18 (ASEE 2026 paper); think-aloud n=6 in both. The gap is not explained; it may be different phases.
limits: Poster text is sparse and partly garbled in extraction. Sample size mismatch unresolved.
agent_relevance: Cite the paper's n=18 as the safer figure. The poster names open questions: how complexity overwhelms novices, and how to change students' stance.

source: Daly, Anand, Abel, Sabuncu (2024) Industry Perspectives on Mechanical Engineering Troubleshooting (ASEE Paper 43448)
finding: Pilot interviews with nine engineers gave three themes: understanding the problem, diagnostic techniques, resource management. Diagnostic techniques were a top-down systematic method, pattern recognition, adaptability, efficiency and decision trees.
numbers: N=9 engineers, 10 to 40 years of experience, interviews 30 to 60 minutes. The diagnostic techniques theme appeared in 22 coded instances. Coding followed Miles and Huberman, with team coding as a reliability check.
limits: N=9; the authors could not establish a stopping criterion (saturation). Interviewees may not have covered all methods. Self-report.
agent_relevance: Experts name pattern recognition and top-down decomposition together. Our agent can pair a case memory (pattern) with a decomposition operator (top-down).
quote: With experience, you start to see patterns... and these patterns guide you towards the root cause.

source: Daly, Anand, Abel, Sabuncu (2024) Industry Perspectives on Mechanical Engineering Troubleshooting (ASEE Paper 43448)
finding: Experts stress understanding design intent and normal operation before diagnosing. A defense engineer described a concept of operations document; a clean-energy engineer used flow charts and logic paths; a data-storage engineer compared field data to drawings and manuals.
numbers: Single-interviewee examples. In a life-critical medical device case, remote monitoring found an abnormal voltage spike unique to the affected device, which avoided a recall.
limits: Anecdotes, not measured effects.
agent_relevance: Add an early step: write what normal operation is and what the design intent is, before generating causes.

source: Daly, Anand, Abel, Sabuncu (2024) Industry Perspectives on Mechanical Engineering Troubleshooting (ASEE Paper 43448)
finding: Engineers value stakeholder input: talk to the customer first about what happened right before the failure, because failures arise when product function and customer assumptions do not align. Multidisciplinary teams and independent design reviews (FDA-mandated in medical devices) help find flaws.
numbers: One interviewee described two novice types: those who ask for help at once and those who never ask and get stuck.
limits: Self-report, N=9. A single LLM agent has no stakeholders unless the task supplies them.
agent_relevance: For our agent the equivalent is: request more evidence when the symptom report is thin, but not everything at once (the 'ask at once' novice type).
quote: Collaboration is not just breaking it up, but it's also not some massive like communal think where everybody has equal weight...

source: Daly, Anand, Abel, Sabuncu (2024) Industry Perspectives on Mechanical Engineering Troubleshooting (ASEE Paper 43448)
finding: The paper offers a seven-phase teaching framework: identification, comprehension, data collection, hypothesis testing, system analysis, identify failure mode, carry out solution. It notes that Structured Troubleshooting (Schaafstal) was not tested against industry norms.
numbers: Framework is a synthesis of 9 interviews plus literature; no outcome test. Tools listed: decision trees, 5 whys, FMEA, root cause analysis, pattern recognition.
limits: Not evaluated with learners.
agent_relevance: A ready list of operators (5 whys, FMEA, decision tree) to compare with our O1 to O8.
quote: ST has not been tested or validated against industry norms and practices.

source: Schaafstal, Schraagen, van Berlo (2000) Cognitive task analysis and innovation of training: the case of structured troubleshooting
finding: Structured Troubleshooting (ST) combines a domain-independent strategy with a context-dependent, multi-level functional decomposition of the system. It came from a cognitive task analysis (two observational studies) to train novice technicians.
numbers: Abstract only (via Crossref): technicians trained in ST solved twice as many malfunctions, in less time, than traditionally trained ones. ST also took less time to teach. Exact N and times not read.
limits: Abstract only; full paper behind a paywall (HTTP 403). Exact numbers unverified.
agent_relevance: Closest founding evidence that a fixed strategy plus functional decomposition beats unguided work. Supports having a scaffold at all.
quote: technicians trained in structured troubleshooting solve twice as many malfunctions, in less time

source: Jonassen and Hung (2006) Learning to troubleshoot: a new theory-based design architecture
finding: Reviews prior troubleshooting instruction and proposes a design architecture: a cognitive model of four tasks (construct the problem space, identify fault systems, diagnose faults, generate and verify solutions), plus remembering experience. Case libraries of past problems anchor learning.
numbers: Secondary summaries only (a reading note and a search summary). Four hypothesis levels reported: system, subsystem, device, component.
limits: Full text not opened. Knowledge-type taxonomy and any empirical data are unverified here.
agent_relevance: The standard cognitive model that the 2026 ASEE project builds on. Check our states S0 to S9 against these four tasks.

source: Dounas-Frazer, Van De Bogart, Stetzer, Lewandowski (2015) The role of modeling in troubleshooting: an example from electronics
finding: Pairs of physics students troubleshot a faulty two-stage cascade amplifier. A 90-second excerpt shows Model Construction, then Prediction, Comparison, Proposal. They used the Split-Half strategy: test the midpoint to isolate the faulty half.
numbers: 16 students (4 pairs at each of 2 universities), junior electronics. Two faults in Stage 2: R3 at 100 ohm instead of 1 kohm, and a burned-out op-amp. Input 100 mV; expected 2 V inverted at Stage 2; measured about 10 mV non-inverted.
limits: One 90-second excerpt analysed in detail. Qualitative. Students, not experts.
agent_relevance: Shows a predict, compare, propose, revise loop with a halving strategy. Without a model of the midpoint the student could not make a prediction: build the model before predicting.

source: Dounas-Frazer, Van De Bogart, Stetzer, Lewandowski (2015) The role of modeling in troubleshooting: an example from electronics
finding: Some reasoning falls outside the modelling framework: negotiation between partners about whether and when to move to the next phase. These are decisions about how to navigate the process.
numbers: Described as common in their data. No count given.
limits: Authors say a complementary framework (socially mediated metacognition) is needed.
agent_relevance: Phase-switch decisions are what our program-controlled transitions do. Supports giving transitions to code, with explicit signals.

source: Chen et al. (2025) AIOpsLab: A holistic framework to evaluate AI agents for enabling autonomous clouds
finding: AIOpsLab: 48 problems testing detection, localization, root cause analysis (RCA) and mitigation of faults in microservice systems. Detection is easiest; RCA and mitigation are hardest. Four LLM agents were compared.
numbers: Detection accuracy: GPT-4 with shell 69.23%, GPT-3.5 with shell 23.07%, ReAct 76.92%, FLASH 100%. Localization Acc@1 (13 problems): GPT-4 61.54%, ReAct 53.85%, FLASH 46.15%. RCA: GPT-4 40.90%, ReAct 45.45%, FLASH 36.36%, GPT-3.5 9.09%. Mitigation: GPT-4 27.27%, GPT-3.5 0%, FLASH 36.36%, ReAct 54.55%.
limits: Small problem set per task (about 11 to 13). Four agents. Simulated microservice apps. Table text extracted with column drift, so a few cells may be misaligned.
agent_relevance: Accuracy falls from detect to localize to explain to fix. A scaffold should spend its budget on RCA and mitigation, and verify mitigation by running a check.

source: Chen et al. (2025) AIOpsLab: A holistic framework to evaluate AI agents for enabling autonomous clouds
finding: Agent behaviour: accuracy rises with the step limit for some agents, then flattens. FLASH reached 59.32% at the best step limit; GPT-3.5 had the lowest overall accuracy, 15.25%. Agents also raised false-positive detections on no-fault problems.
numbers: Overall accuracy FLASH 59.32% (best), GPT-3.5 15.25% (lowest). Only GPT-4 with shell handled the no-fault (noop) case correctly for the microservice apps, per the paper text. Most actions were a few commands (submit, kubectl get).
limits: Details read from text and figures; per-agent counts not all recorded.
agent_relevance: Do not assume more steps always help; add a stop rule and a negative-control check (is there really a fault?).

source: Jha et al. (2025) ITBench: Evaluating AI agents across diverse real-world IT automation tasks
finding: ITBench: 94 real-world IT automation scenarios across SRE, CISO and FinOps. Agents on frontier models resolved few: 13.8% of SRE scenarios, 25.2% of CISO scenarios and 0% of FinOps scenarios.
numbers: 94 scenarios; difficulty split 24% easy, 24% medium, 52% hard. GPT-4o best on SRE: diagnosed 36%, 7.73% and 5.0% of easy, medium and hard; mitigated 21%, 12.27% and 0.0%. No model mitigated any hard scenario in any run.
limits: Models tested were 2024 vintage (granite-3.1-8B, llama-3.1-8B, llama-3.3-70B, GPT-4o). Newer models may do better. Non-deterministic environments.
agent_relevance: The clearest direct measure that complexity hurts: success drops sharply with scenario complexity. Expect low success on hard multi-fault cases and report difficulty.
quote: agents powered by state-of-the-art models resolve only 13.8% of SRE scenarios, 25.2% of CISO scenarios, and 0% of FinOps scenarios

source: Jha et al. (2025) ITBench: Evaluating AI agents across diverse real-world IT automation tasks
finding: Run-to-run variability is large: the same SRE agent on the same scenario diagnosed correctly in only some runs. Removing trace data cut success: GPT-4o diagnosis pass@1 fell from 13.81% to 9.52%, and mitigation fell to 2.86%.
numbers: SRE agent with GPT-4o over 10 runs: scenario 13 diagnosed 6/10, scenario 8 1/10, scenario 21 8/10. Mitigated: scenario 16 6/10, scenario 8 2/10, scenario 21 5/10.
limits: 10 runs per scenario. The environment is itself non-deterministic, so variance mixes model and environment.
agent_relevance: Single-run accuracy is unreliable; measure with repeated runs (supports G4). Which evidence is available (traces) changes outcomes strongly.

source: Roy et al. (2024) Exploring LLM-based Agents for Root Cause Analysis
finding: A ReAct agent with retrieval tools was compared with chain-of-thought and retrieval baselines for incident root causes at a large IT company. ReAct was competitive on correctness but had far fewer hallucinations. Adding human discussion text from the incident did not significantly help.
numbers: Correctness 35% for ReAct (BM25 search) vs 39% for the baselines (CoT and RB k=10). Hallucination: 4% for ReAct vs 12% for CoT and 40% for RB. About 2 lookups per incident. 28 of 97 examples solved by all three.
limits: Out-of-distribution production incidents from one company. ReAct did not beat baselines on correctness.
agent_relevance: Tools bought factual grounding, not more correct answers. Fits G2: revise from real output.

source: Gao et al. (2023) Automatic Root Cause Analysis via Large Language Models for Cloud Incidents (RCACopilot)
finding: RCACopilot routes incidents to handlers by alert type, collects diagnostic data, predicts a root-cause category and writes an explanation. The data-collection part has run in production at Microsoft for over four years.
numbers: Accuracy up to 0.766 on a year of real Microsoft incidents. Incident count not recorded here.
limits: Abstract and introduction read, not the full tables. Category prediction, not free-form diagnosis. Internal data.
agent_relevance: A hand-written expert collection procedure per alert type, then an LLM summarises. Expert procedure plus LLM may beat free LLM reasoning.

source: Wang et al. (2024) RCAgent: Cloud Root Cause Analysis by Autonomous Agents with Tool-Augmented LLMs (CIKM)
finding: A tool-augmented agent with action-trajectory self-consistency and context management beats ReAct for cloud RCA on Alibaba Flink, judged by metrics and humans. Without key components, the pass rate falls sharply.
numbers: Full system: 99.38% pass rate within 15 steps, 7.93% invalid rate. One ablation lowered pass rate by 33.54% with a 70.95% invalid rate; another collapsed to 70.19% pass and 44.80% invalid. Responsibility judgment about 82.06%.
limits: Internal model, not public. Pass rate measures valid format more than truth. Partial reading.
agent_relevance: Big gains came from stabilising the agent loop (context management, trajectory voting), not only the model. Note G4: voting among one model's samples is not independent.

source: Pham et al. (2025) RCAEval: A Benchmark for Root Cause Analysis of Microservice Systems with Telemetry Data
finding: A benchmark of 735 failure cases from three microservice systems with 15 reproducible baselines for coarse and fine-grained RCA. Built because earlier studies tested on only 1 to 2 systems and 2 to 3 fault types.
numbers: 735 failure cases; 3 datasets; 15 baselines. The authors criticise one earlier dataset (Eadro) for an unrealistic load of 2 to 3 requests per second.
limits: Not an LLM study; classical RCA baselines. Abstract and introduction read.
agent_relevance: Narrow test sets inflate accuracy. Use many fault types when testing our own troubleshooting scaffold.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) Automated Root Causing of Cloud Incidents using In-Context Learning with GPT-4
finding: In-context learning with retrieved similar incidents beat fine-tuned GPT-3 on root-cause generation over 100,000+ production incidents, with a human check by incident owners.
numbers: On average 24.8% better than fine-tuned GPT-3 across metrics and 49.7% better than zero-shot. Incident-owner ratings: 43.5% better correctness and 8.7% better readability than the fine-tuned model.
limits: Abstract and introduction read. Company data, not public. Relative gains only.
agent_relevance: Retrieving similar past cases lifts accuracy: supports a case library, also what Jonassen and Hung propose for human learners.
